bava_metzia-23b-8-8.note: A man found pitch near a winepress and came to ask Rav what to do with it. Rav told him to take it for himself. Seeing the man still hesitate, Rav said: go and share it with my son Hiyya, showing he was sure it was not stolen property.
bava_metzia-23b-8-8.why: The discussion asks whether the place where an item is found counts as a mark that lets the owner reclaim it. Rav's ruling seems to say no, but Rabbi Abba explains it otherwise: grass had grown through the pitch, so its owner had long given up on it.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Founder of the great academy at Sura in Babylonia, one of the most important early Sages of the Talmud.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: A Sage who explains the reasoning behind Rav's ruling.

terms.meaning: A feature an owner can describe to prove a lost item is his. A finder must announce items that have one; items without one may often be kept.
Once an owner has given up hope of getting a lost item back, it becomes ownerless and the finder may keep it.

bava_metzia-24b-10-10.note: Two short cases of found property. Rabbi Ami found slaughtered young birds on the road between Tiberias and Tzippori and asked what to do; the reports differ on whether he asked Rabbi Asi, Rabbi Yoḥanan or the study hall, but the answer was: take them for yourself. Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa found a skein of thread used for weaving nets, asked Rabbi Yoḥanan or the study hall, and got the same answer, because he found it in a place where crowds pass.
bava_metzia-24b-10-10.why: The Gemara is collecting rulings in which Sages let a finder keep lost meat and goods found in public places, following Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view; these two cases continue that series right after the similar case of Rabbi Ḥanina's slaughtered goat on the same road.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel, student of Rabbi Yoḥanan, who found the slaughtered birds.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel and close colleague of Rabbi Ami.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The foremost Sage of the Land of Israel in his generation, head of the academy in Tiberias.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel; his name means 'the smith'. He found the skein of thread.

terms.meaning: The house of study where Sages met to learn and decide questions of law together.

bava_metzia-44b-4-4.note: Rav borrowed gold dinars from the daughter of Rabbi Hiyya. By the time he came to repay, gold dinars had risen in value, and Rav worried that returning them would mean paying her interest. He went to Rabbi Hiyya, who told him: go and pay her back in good, full-weight dinars.
bava_metzia-44b-4-4.why: The Gemara is asking whether gold coins count as money or as goods compared with silver, and reads this ruling as showing Rabbi Hiyya treated gold as money. It then rejects the proof: Rav had dinars of his own elsewhere, which changes the case.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Founder of the academy at Sura in Babylonia; he had studied in the Land of Israel and was related to Rabbi Hiyya.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A leading Sage of the generation after the Mishna, Rav's teacher and uncle.

terms.meaning: The Torah forbids a Jew to pay or take any extra on a loan to another Jew, including repaying goods that have gone up in value.
A measure of volume for grain and produce. Lending a se'a of produce and getting a se'a back is forbidden, because prices may rise in between.

bava_metzia-69b-5-5.note: Abba Mar, the son of Rav Pappa, used to accept pans of wax from wax makers and then ask his father to lend them money. The Sages complained to Rav Pappa that his son was taking interest. Rav Pappa replied that interest of this kind is fine: the Torah forbids only interest that passes from borrower to lender, and his son was simply being paid for putting in a word.
bava_metzia-69b-5-5.why: Rava has just ruled that a person may take a fee for asking someone else to make a loan; this case shows the ruling in practice.

people.name: Abba Mar
people.about: Son of Rav Pappa, who earned wax for arranging loans from his father.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A leading Babylonian Sage, head of an academy at Naresh.

terms.meaning: The Torah forbids a lender to take any extra from a Jewish borrower in return for a loan.

bava_metzia-84a-8-9.note: Rabbi Yoḥanan, famous for his beauty, used to sit at the entrance of the ritual bath. He explained that Jewish women coming out after their monthly immersion should see him first, so that they would have children as beautiful and as learned in Torah as he was. The Rabbis asked whether he was not afraid of the evil eye. He answered that he was descended from Joseph, whom the evil eye cannot harm, citing a verse about Joseph as Rabbi Abbahu read it.
bava_metzia-84a-8-9.why: The Gemara has been describing the bodies and beauty of the Sages, especially the beauty of Rabbi Yoḥanan. This story continues that theme, and the discussion goes on to give another source for why Joseph's descendants are safe from the evil eye.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The foremost Sage of the Land of Israel in his generation, remembered in the Talmud for his striking beauty.

people.name: Joseph
people.about: Son of Jacob in the Bible. Rabbi Yoḥanan claims descent from him.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel and student of Rabbi Yoḥanan, whose reading of the verse is quoted.

terms.meaning: A pool of water a woman immerses in after her monthly period, before she and her husband may resume relations.
The belief that envy or an admiring gaze can cause harm, so that drawing attention to one's good fortune is dangerous.
A way the Sages teach from a verse by reading one word slightly differently, here turning 'by a fountain' into 'rising above the eye'.

bava_metzia-85b-4-4.note: Rabbi Ḥanina and Rabbi Ḥiyya used to argue over Torah, and each would tell the other he was no match for him. Rabbi Ḥanina boasted that if the Torah were ever forgotten by the Jewish people, he could rebuild it through his own sharp reasoning. Rabbi Ḥiyya answered that he was the one making sure the Torah would never be forgotten in the first place. The Gemara goes on to let him explain how he did it.
bava_metzia-85b-4-4.why: The Gemara has just told of a Divine Voice saying Reish Lakish analyzed Torah like Rabbi Ḥiyya but did not spread it as he did. This exchange contrasts brilliance in argument with the work of keeping Torah alive, and Rabbi Ḥiyya's account of his teaching follows.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: Rabbi Ḥanina bar Ḥama, a Sage of the Land of Israel and student of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, known for his sharp reasoning.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: A great Sage who lived in the Land of Israel around 200 CE, known for his role in preserving and teaching the Mishna.
